image.altEn: Spanish-language xkcd comic #361: Christmas Back Home

titleText.es: Que la familia se vaya a la cama a las 10 PM es mucho peor que el jet lag.
titleText.en: Family going to bed at 10 PM is so much worse than jet lag.
titleText.noteEn: The title text extends the joke by comparing the family's early holiday bedtime with the disruption of jet lag.

regions.labelEs: ERA NOCHEBUENA EN CASA DE MI FAMILIA.
NO HABÍA NINGÚN SONIDO, EXCEPTO EL CLIC DE UN RATÓN.

applications.explanationEn: No remains before había because ningún supplies a matching negative before the masculine noun sonido.

regions.labelEs: PORQUE ERA COMO LA NAVIDAD DE UN NIÑO, EXCEPTO
QUE HABÍA OLVIDADO LA HORA A LA QUE DUERME LA GENTE NORMAL.

applications.explanationEn: Había is the helper form, and olvidado is the unchanged completed-action form of olvidar.
A supplies the time relationship, la matches the feminine noun hora, and que links back to that noun.
Qué and haces form the surprised question frame, and levantado supplies the unexpected condition.
Tan immediately precedes the adverb tarde and intensifies how late the time is.

excludedUnits.rationale: This is the numerical clock hour, not a printed Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Son is the plural clock-time form and las is the matching feminine plural article used before the hour number.

cards.noteEn: Era is a past form of ser used for a background state, description, or ongoing past situation. This form is called the imperfect.

cards.promptEs: Nochebuena · ningún sonido · clic de un ratón
cards.answerEn: The narration parodies the famous Christmas poem commonly called 'Twas the Night Before Christmas.
cards.noteEn: The poem opens on Christmas Eve and describes a house so quiet that not even a mouse is stirring. The comic replaces that quiet animal with the click of a computer mouse, then has Santa find someone awake at three in the morning.

cards.questionEn: Why can a Spanish sentence contain both no and another negative word?
cards.answerEn: When the second negative word follows the verb, keep no before the verb too.
cards.noteEn: Spanish commonly uses matching negative words together. No tiene ninguna means “it does not have any”; it does not become a positive meaning as two negatives sometimes do in formal English.

example.en: I do not have any doubt.

cards.noteEn: This past form of hay presents something as existing in a past setting. In this use, había stays singular even before a plural noun: había una silla and había dos sillas.

example.es: Había dos cartas en la mesa.
example.en: There were two letters on the table.

cards.answerEn: no; not any (before a masculine singular noun)
cards.noteEn: Ningún is used directly before a masculine singular noun. When it comes after the verb, Spanish normally also keeps no before the verb: no tengo ningún problema.

example.en: We did not see any error.

cards.noteEn: Sonido can mean sound in general or a particular noise that can be heard.
Ratón can name either the animal or a computer mouse. Words about clicking or a computer normally select the device meaning.

example.es: Muevo el cursor con el ratón.
example.en: I move the cursor with the mouse.

cards.noteEn: Unaccented como can introduce the person, thing, or situation used for a comparison. It does not ask “how”; the question word cómo has an accent.
Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: had (helper for an earlier completed action)
cards.noteEn: Before a completed-action form such as escrito, había is a past form of the helper haber. It places one completed action before another point in the past.

example.en: I had already eaten when you called.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something had already happened before another past moment?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching past form of haber, then the action verb's completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: Use había for I, he, she, or one thing; habías for informal singular “you”; habíamos for “we”; habíais for informal plural “you” in Spain; and habían for “they” or plural formal “you.” The second verb uses a completed-action form, called a past participle: most -ar verbs end in -ado and most -er or -ir verbs end in -ido, although some are irregular, such as escribir → escrito. Only haber changes for the person; the completed-action form stays unchanged.

example.es: Ya habíamos terminado cuando llegó Luis.
example.en: We had already finished when Luis arrived.

cards.noteEn: Olvidado is the completed-action form of olvidar, “to forget.” It follows a form of haber in perfect constructions.

cards.answerEn: at; links hora to la que ('at which')
cards.noteEn: A supplies the time relationship before la que. English may place the matching 'at' earlier or at the end, but Spanish keeps it before la que.

example.es: No sé la hora a la que abre el museo.
example.en: I do not know the time at which the museum opens.

cards.questionEn: How do you say forms such as “in which,” “with whom,” or “for whom” when referring back to a person or thing?
cards.answerEn: Put the needed preposition before el que, la que, los que, or las que, matching the earlier person or thing.
cards.noteEn: A preposition is a short relationship word such as en (“in”), con (“with”), or para (“for”). Choose el, la, los, or las to match the gender and number of the person or thing being described; que itself does not change. English may use “which” for a thing or “who” or “whom” for a person.

example.es: Esta es la silla en la que me siento.
example.en: This is the chair that I sit in.

cards.answerEn: the feminine article in la que; helps mean which, who, or whom

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.noteEn: Duerme is the present form of dormir used with one person or thing. Spanish treats gente, 'people,' as grammatically singular, so gente goes with duerme rather than duermen.

example.es: La gente duerme poco en verano.

cards.promptEs: ¿qué + forma de hacer + lugar o estado?
cards.questionEn: How do you ask why someone is in an unexpected place or condition?
cards.answerEn: Begin with qué and the appropriate form of hacer, then add the place or the word that describes the person's condition.
cards.noteEn: The question literally asks what the person is doing, but it can express surprise at finding that person there or in that condition. Hacer changes for the person: hago means 'I do,' haces means 'you do,' and hace means 'he, she, or formal you does.'
Levantado describes a male person who is awake and no longer in bed. Its ending changes to levantada for a female person and to levantados or levantadas for a plural group.

cards.questionEn: How do you intensify a describing word to mean “so,” as in “so difficult”?
cards.answerEn: Put tan immediately before the word that describes the person, thing, or action.
cards.noteEn: Tan does not change form. It goes before an adjective, a word that describes a person or thing, or before an adverb, a word that describes an action. Use forms of tanto instead before a noun or when saying “so much” or “so many.”
Son normally means 'they are,' but clock time uses son before every hour except one o'clock because the understood word horas is plural.

cards.promptEs: es la una · son las dos, tres...
cards.questionEn: How do you state the clock time in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Use es la for one o'clock and son las for every other hour.
cards.noteEn: Es and son are forms of ser, 'to be.' Spanish treats one o'clock as singular, es la una, and the other hours as plural, son las dos, son las tres, and so on. The feminine article la or las appears because hora or horas is understood.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; used before plural clock hours
cards.noteEn: The understood word is horas, a feminine plural noun, so Spanish uses las before two o'clock and every later hour. One o'clock instead uses la: es la una.

example.es: La clase empieza a las nueve.
